particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, charges, sentence lengths, compensation amount and the book title are omitted.

items.record: The witness hesitated at first, then the police procedure firmed up her choice: "it is between number four and number five", and only after a second viewing with spoken phrases did she pick number five.
items.reading: A confident eyewitness whose account was "shaped by nobody" and whose certainty was settled from the start.
items.loss: The reading misses how an uncertain identification was made firm through repeated police lineups.

items.record: The suspect entered the photo pool because of an earlier record: police showed mugshots including one of a man "arrested as a teenager for breaking and entering".
items.loss: The reading misses how a prior record drew the defendant into the suspect pool to begin with.

items.record: A second victim twice failed to identify him, then at retrial named him, "saying she had been too afraid to identify him right after the crime."
items.loss: The reading misses a second witness whose testimony changed over time, from no identification to an accusation.

items.record: Physical evidence that looked consistent backed up the mistake: foam insoles "that appeared similar" and a flashlight that "resembled" the attacker's.
items.reading: Forensic error is offered only as an alternative source, not as material that supported the eyewitness.
items.loss: The reading misses how loosely matching circumstantial evidence combined with the eyewitness account to strengthen the false conclusion.

items.record: The trial judge excluded evidence that another victim had picked a different man: "The trial court excluded the evidence on grounds that it was not relevant."
items.reading: It describes passive suppression mostly after conviction, through procedural denials.
items.loss: The reading misses active exclusion of evidence that pointed away from the defendant, at the trial itself.

items.record: The appellate court corrected that error in the defendant's favor: the high court "reversed the convictions and ordered a new trial."
items.reading: Years of drifting filings, with every denial explaining why the record still holds.
items.loss: The reading gets wrong how the institution behaved, since a higher court actually sided with the defendant before the case went wrong again.

items.record: The retrial made things worse rather than fixing them: he was "charged with both rapes" and was convicted of more counts.
items.loss: The reading misses the sequence in which a successful appeal led to a heavier second conviction.

items.record: The real perpetrator was known and was screened out by the victims outside the jury's presence: "Ms. Thompson-Cannino and the other woman both contended that he was not their attacker", so he could not be presented as an alternative suspect.
items.loss: The reading misses that the true offender was already in the courtroom and was excluded because the witnesses rejected him.

items.record: The true perpetrator had confessed informally: "he had admitted to other inmates that he had committed both crimes."
items.loss: The reading misses a confession that circulated in prison and never reached the official process.

items.record: The defense asked for testing and the police complied: police "turned over all physical evidence" at the defense's request, and the DNA database matched the other man.
items.reading: Grudging exoneration driven by outside pressure that keeps compounding: press coverage, an innocence project, a recantation.
items.loss: The reading misdescribes how the exoneration happened, which was a cooperative handover of evidence rather than a reaction to mounting outside pressure.

items.record: The prosecution joined in the dismissal, a pardon followed, and the real offender pleaded guilty: "The district attorney and the defense filed a motion to dismiss all charges".
items.reading: A face-saving negotiated outcome such as an Alford plea, framed so the court is not admitting error.
items.loss: The reading gets the resolution wrong, since it was a full joint dismissal, a pardon and a guilty plea by the real offender.

items.record: Accuser and exonerated man reconciled and became advocates together: "They became good friends and began to travel around the country to speak about wrongful convictions."
items.reading: absent; the witness's reaction is listed only as unknowable inner experience.
items.loss: The reading misses that the relationship between the accuser and the accused turned into a partnership for reform.

items.record: Life after release was rebuilt partly through the institution that proved his innocence: "got a job in the warehouse of LabCorp, the company that tested the DNA evidence."
items.loss: The reading misses how the defendant rebuilt his life after release, including state compensation and family.
